Suzuki T2D

This vignette asks whether gpmapr’s univariate SNP programs recover the mechanistic clusters of type 2 diabetes (T2D) signals that Suzuki et al. (2024) defined. The analysis runs on the European-ancestry meta-analysis from that paper, uploaded to GPMap. The questions are:

  • Which programs pass validation? Only high and medium confidence programs are compared with Suzuki’s clusters.
  • Do a program’s member SNPs match the index SNVs of a Suzuki cluster?
  • Does its profile over Suzuki’s cardiometabolic traits match the cluster’s?
  • Does it carry that cluster’s canonical genes?

The program summary cards in Part 4 bring these together, and Part 4 ends with a hand-written match of each program to Suzuki’s clusters.

Part 1: Suzuki et al. (2024)

Suzuki K, Hatzikotoulas K, Southam L, et al. Genetic drivers of heterogeneity in type 2 diabetes pathophysiology. Nature 627, 347–357 (2024). https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-024-07019-6

The reference tables used below are CC BY 4.0 extracts of the paper’s supplementary material. They are in inst/extdata/suzuki2024/ and are regenerated by data-raw/suzuki2024.R.

Study

  • Scale. The Type 2 Diabetes Global Genomics Initiative meta-analysed 428,452 T2D cases and 2,107,149 controls across six ancestry groups.
  • Discovery. Signals come from multi-ancestry meta-regression (MR-MEGA) with three axes of genetic variation as covariates.
    • Index SNVs were selected at P < 5 × 10⁻⁸ by greedy clumping. A variant joined a clump if r² > 0.05 with the index SNV in any of the five 1000 Genomes super-populations, within 5 Mb.
    • This gave 1,289 independent signals at 611 loci, of which 145 loci are new.
  • EUR meta-analysis (the dataset used here).
    • 36 GWAS: 242,283 cases and 1,569,734 controls (effective N ≈ 751,755, 60.3% of the total).
    • Fixed-effects inverse-variance meta-analysis in METAL, GRCh37.
    • The largest contributors are the Million Veteran Program (90,107 cases), FinnGen (37,002), UK Biobank (19,119), the Estonian Biobank (12,208) and deCODE (11,448). 23andMe is not included.
  • Signal sets differ. The 1,289 signals were discovered in the multi-ancestry analysis, so some are driven by non-European data and may be weak or absent in the EUR upload.

How the clusters were built

  1. Inputs. Each index SNV’s associations with 37 cardiometabolic traits were taken from the largest available GWAS (Supplementary Table 5) and aligned to the T2D risk allele.
  2. Scaling. Each association was scaled as \(Z_{ij} = \beta_{ij} / (\sqrt{N_i}\, s_{ij})\), which is a standardised per-allele effect that does not depend on the trait GWAS’s size.
  3. Clustering. The SNVs were grouped by k-means with iterative imputation of missing associations (ClustImpute). The number of clusters came from the majority rule over 27 NbClust indices.
  4. Hard assignment. Every SNV is assigned to exactly one cluster. This differs from earlier soft clustering by Bayesian non-negative matrix factorisation (Udler et al. 2018), which gives each SNV cluster weights and leaves some unassigned.
The eight mechanistic clusters (main-text Table 1, Supplementary Table 9, Fig. 2). * = trait adjusted for BMI. t2d_or is the inverse-variance weighted mean T2D odds ratio of the cluster’s index SNVs. Insulin secretion/sensitivity give the direction of the T2D risk allele’s effect.

How the paper validated the clusters

  • Physiology. The clusters form a cline in insulin-related measures (HOMA-B, HOMA-IR, clamp-derived sensitivity). It runs from low insulin secretion in the two beta-cell clusters to the most extreme insulin resistance in the Lipodystrophy cluster.
  • Single-cell open chromatin. The clusters are enriched for different cell types:
    • beta-cell and Residual glycaemic clusters: pancreatic islets;
    • Beta cell −PI: also enterochromaffin cells;
    • Lipodystrophy: adipocytes only;
    • Metabolic syndrome: pericytes and endothelial cells;
    • Obesity: islet non-beta cells, adrenal and brain neurons;
    • Body fat: no enrichment.
  • Partitioned polygenic scores. After adjusting for the overall T2D score:
    • the Obesity score is associated with higher risk of coronary artery disease, peripheral artery disease, end-stage diabetic nephropathy and earlier T2D onset;
    • the Beta cell +PI score is associated with lower coronary artery disease and nephropathy risk.

Caveats for using the clusters as a benchmark

  • They are one partition, not ground truth. They come from one algorithm on one trait panel.
  • Two clusters act as catch-alls. Residual glycaemic (389 signals) and Body fat (273) are the largest. Body fat has no chromatin enrichment, and the three new clusters have weaker T2D effects than the established ones.
  • Liver/lipid metabolism has only 3 signals. Its chromatin model was unstable in the paper, and it is not a realistic target for recovery.
  • Hard assignment forces membership. SNVs with intermediate profiles still get a cluster, whereas gpmapr’s EBMF programs are soft and overlapping.

Part 3: Univariate analysis

The steps are the same as in the univariate analysis investigation, except that T2D proxy traits are removed first (see below):

  1. Build a pleiotropy matrix of z-scores (beta / se) for every background trait at each upload SNP, keeping phenotypic traits only and leaving out the T2D proxy traits.
  2. Drop sparse traits (observed at fewer than min_snp_signals SNPs) and ubiquitous traits (observed at more than 80% of SNPs).
  3. Orient every SNP to the T2D risk allele and compress with asinh.
  4. Factorise with EBMF into overlapping programs.
  5. Validate the programs.

Shared settings come from vignettes/_ebmf_settings.yml. After validation, each program is annotated as in that vignette, in one table:

  • module-specific traits;
  • loading-based (continuous) enrichment of trait categories, tissues and pathways;
  • the genes at the program’s SNPs, which this vignette adds (shown in the program summary cards).

Only the pleiotropy comparison of unique vs shared SNPs is left to the univariate vignette.

T2D proxy traits

GPMap holds several other GWAS of T2D itself, or of traits defined by having diabetes. At risk-oriented T2D SNPs they all repeat the anchor trait, so they add no information about mechanism. They can also give EBMF extra weight to spend on small differences between near-identical rows. They are removed from the matrix before fitting.

The list was drawn up by searching all_traits() and the upload’s coloc partners for diabetes-related names, then pruned by hand. It covers:

  • T2D GWAS: GPMap’s own T2D and the UK Biobank SPA/Firth versions.
  • Diagnosis: doctor-diagnosed, self-reported and ICD10 E11.9 diabetes.
  • Treatment: diabetes medication, metformin, gliclazide and insulin.
  • Family history: diabetes in the mother, father or siblings.
  • Complications: diabetes-related eye disease.

Kept on purpose:

  • Glycaemic traits (glucose, HbA1c, insulin and proinsulin), which are Suzuki clustering traits.
  • Type 1 diabetes, a distinct disease.
  • Combined medication fields, such as “Medication for cholesterol, blood pressure or diabetes: Blood pressure medication”.

Program confidence

summarise_ebmf_programs() drops programs with fewer than min_module_size member SNPs and gives every other program a confidence tier. Every kept program is annotated in Part 3, whatever its tier; Part 4 compares only the high and medium programs with Suzuki’s clusters.

Member SNPs are those passing the lFSR/magnitude cut. S is the cosine similarity between two SNPs’ oriented, compressed profiles across the background traits, with missing cells counted as 0 and the T2D row left out (it is positive at every SNP, so it would add the same similarity to every pair).

  • low — similarity_q >= similarity_q: the member SNPs are no more alike than random SNP groups of the same size. This is checked first, so a program that fails it is low whatever its number of traits, and can be set aside.
  • single_trait — passes the similarity test, but the program’s trait loadings rest on fewer than min_effective_traits effective traits. A program is defined as multi-trait: a factor carried by one trait is just that trait’s hits, which noise produces too, so it needs a closer look rather than being discarded.
  • high — similarity_q < high_similarity_q and connectedness >= high_connectedness.
  • medium — similarity_q < similarity_q, but not high.

The columns:

  • effective_n_traits: 1 / sum(p^2), where p are the program’s squared trait loadings as shares of their total (T2D row left out): 1 for a program on one trait, n for n equally loaded traits.

  • mean_internal_similarity and similarity_q: the mean S between pairs of member SNPs, and the BH-adjusted share of random groups of the same number of T2D SNPs that are at least as similar. A significance test, so larger programs pass more easily.

  • connectedness: the share of member pairs with S >= similarity_threshold.

  • excess_similarity and excess_connectedness (reported): each of the above minus its value in the random groups; effect sizes that do not grow with program size.

  • factor_pve_pct (reported): the share of the matrix variance the factor explains.

  • replication (reported): the mean Jaccard overlap between the program’s top SNPs and the best-matching factor when 20% of the background traits are held out and EBMF is refit.

  • parent_program: when at least 90% of a program’s SNPs sit at the loci of a larger program, that program is its parent. Sub-programs are kept and listed under their parent.

Module-specific traits and loading-based enrichment

One row per analysed program, in confidence order (green high, orange medium, grey single trait, red low), with each child program indented under its parent. The columns come from two analyses.

Module-specific traits. The background traits most elevated in the program relative to the rest of the T2D SNPs: specificity = mean |z| in program / (mean |z| elsewhere + 0.1), shown in brackets. Traits need a specificity of at least 1.25, and the top 8 are listed.

Loading-based enrichment of trait categories, tissues and pathways (KEGG and Reactome, on the colocalising QTL genes). There is no membership cutoff: every SNP contributes to every program, weighted by its squared EBMF loading, in the regression lm(loading^2 ~ membership). A hit needs both FDR ≤ 0.05 and R² ≥ 0.05. The FDR is computed across every program tested, separately for categories, tissues and pathways.

Tissues differ from Suzuki’s. GPMap’s tissues are GTEx-style bulk tissues. “Pancreas” is bulk GTEx pancreas, mostly exocrine, and there are no islets. Suzuki’s islet-cell enrichments therefore have no direct counterpart here.

Part 4: Do the programs recapture Suzuki’s clusters?

Expectations (written before the results)

  • Likely to be recovered: Obesity, Lipodystrophy and Metabolic syndrome. Their defining traits (BMI, WHR, body fat %, TG, HDL, blood pressure) are large UK Biobank GWAS with hundreds of coloc groups in GPMap.
  • Not expected: the Beta cell +PI / −PI split. The two clusters differ mainly in the sign of the proinsulin effect. GPMap’s proinsulin GWAS has N = 10,701 and 12 coloc groups, so a joint beta-cell program would be the realistic outcome.
  • Glycaemic clusters lean on HbA1c. Fasting glucose, fasting insulin and 2-hour glucose are sparse in GPMap, so HbA1c carries most of the glycaemic signal.
  • Body fat vs Obesity may merge. They differ mainly on abdominal subcutaneous and visceral fat, which have only 2–7 coloc groups in GPMap.
  • Liver/lipid metabolism (3 signals) is not expected.
  • Tissues. A Lipodystrophy-like program should be enriched in adipose, an Obesity-like program possibly in brain or hypothalamus (Suzuki found brain neurons), and a liver program in liver. Beta-cell programs are not expected to show pancreas: GPMap has no islet QTLs.

Part 4 compares only the high and medium confidence programs with Suzuki’s clusters. Low and single-trait programs are listed in Part 3 but are not interpreted here. The comparison has five parts, after a check of which Suzuki traits the matrix contains:

  • 4b: Suzuki’s canonical marker genes, found positionally and through colocalising QTLs.
  • 4c: each Suzuki index SNV, matched to the GPMap SNP in its LD block, and the programs that SNP ended up in.
  • 4d: each program’s mean profile over the Suzuki clustering traits, compared with each cluster’s profile.
  • 4e: one summary card per program.
  • 4f: a hand-written reading of which program matches which cluster, using 4c–4e together.

4a. Trait coverage

The univariate matrix already contains every phenotypic GPMap trait that colocalises with the upload’s SNPs. trait_map.csv records which of those rows are Suzuki’s 37 clustering traits:

  • same_gwas: the GWAS Suzuki used;
  • proxy: a different GWAS of the same trait;
  • unadjusted_proxy: Suzuki used a BMI-adjusted trait and GPMap has it unadjusted;
  • none: no GPMap equivalent.

Nothing extra is fetched or fitted for these traits.

4b. Canonical marker genes

The example loci that Suzuki et al. give for each cluster (Table 1) are checked against the genes at the member SNPs of each high or medium program, in two ways:

  • positional: the gene is the nearest protein-coding gene to one of the program’s SNPs, which is how Suzuki named the locus;
  • QTL: the gene’s molecular QTL colocalises with one of the program’s SNPs.

A gene found neither way is labelled “low / single-trait program only” if it is at a member SNP of a program outside those tiers, “at a matrix SNP, not in a program” if some SNP in the pleiotropy matrix carries it, and “not found” otherwise. “Not found” usually means the locus has no upload signal that colocalises with enough traits to enter the matrix (see 4c).

4c. Suzuki index SNVs in the programs

Suzuki’s clusters are sets of index SNVs, so the most direct comparison is at the SNP level. Gene names are not enough for this: Suzuki’s 1,289 signals sit at 611 named loci, and 201 of those loci have signals in more than one cluster (TCF7L2 has 32 signals across four clusters).

Each Suzuki index SNV is matched to the upload as follows:

  • Position. The SNV’s GRCh38 position (pos_b38 in index_snv_clusters.csv, looked up by rsid in Ensembl) places it in a GPMap LD block. GPMap colocalises within LD blocks, so this is the unit a signal lives in.
  • Match. The SNV is matched to the pleiotropy-matrix SNP in the same LD block, taking the nearest one if the block has several. The two are usually different variants: GPMap’s lead variant comes from its own fine-mapping of the EUR upload, while Suzuki’s index SNV comes from the multi-ancestry meta-regression.
  • Status. Each SNV then ends up in one of five places: no upload signal in its LD block; an upload signal that is not in the matrix (it colocalises with too few traits); in the matrix but in no program; in low or single-trait programs only; or in at least one high or medium program.

Several Suzuki SNVs, sometimes from different clusters, can match the same GPMap SNP. In the per-program counts below, each matched GPMap SNP counts once, split evenly across the SNVs it matches: a SNP matched by two Obesity SNVs and one Body fat SNV adds 2/3 to Obesity and 1/3 to Body fat.

The table below counts, for each high or medium program, the Suzuki clusters of the index SNVs matched to its member SNPs (split as described above). The first row is the same count over every matched SNP in the matrix, which is what a program with no preference for any cluster would look like.

  • enrichment: a cluster’s share of the program’s matched SNPs divided by its share of all matched SNPs.
  • q: the share of 2,000 random sets of matched SNPs, of the program’s size, with at least the program’s count for that cluster; BH-adjusted over every program × cluster cell.
  • top_cluster: the cluster with the smallest p, among clusters with at least two matched SNPs in the program. A top cluster with q above 0.05 is no evidence of a preference.

4d. Trait-profile similarity

Suzuki’s clusters are defined by their profiles over 37 cardiometabolic traits. This compares those profiles directly with each program’s.

  • Program profile: the mean of the EBMF input matrix over the program’s member SNPs, on the Suzuki traits that are rows of the matrix (4a). This is the matrix EBMF factorises: each SNP is aligned to its T2D risk allele, as in Suzuki’s profiles, and the z-scores are asinh-compressed. A missing cell (no colocalisation) counts as 0. (, the raw matrix, is not aligned, so its column means would mix risk and protective alleles.)
  • Cluster profile: Suzuki’s cluster mean, as beta / se (Supplementary Table 7).
  • Similarity: the cosine between the two profiles over the shared traits: 1 for the same pattern of signs and relative sizes, 0 for unrelated, −1 for opposite.

The two profiles are on different scales (asinh-compressed colocalisation z against the z of a cluster mean), so only the pattern is compared, not the size. A program that loads on few of the Suzuki traits gets a noisy cosine. Some Suzuki clusters have similar profiles over these traits, so a program cannot separate them; the first table gives the cosine between the clusters themselves as a reference.

4e. Program summary cards

One row per high (green) or medium (orange) program, by confidence tier and then by similarity, with each child program indented under its parent:

  • effective_n_traits: how many traits the program’s loadings are spread over (see Program confidence in Part 3).
  • specific_traits: the top three module-specific traits.
  • tissues and pathways: the top three loading-based hits (FDR ≤ 0.05 and R² ≥ 0.05, largest effect first; Part 3).
  • suzuki_snvs: the Suzuki clusters of the index SNVs matched to the program’s member SNPs (4c), largest first.
  • suzuki_loci: those SNVs’ loci (Suzuki’s names), with the clusters of the SNVs at each (×n for several SNVs), strongest loading first. Several clusters at one locus means Suzuki had several signals there that GPMap resolves as one.
  • profile_match: the Suzuki cluster whose trait profile is closest to the program’s (4d), with the cosine.
  • genes: the first 10 positional and QTL genes, strongest loading first. Genes in bold are named at a Suzuki et al. index SNV.

4f. Matching programs to Suzuki clusters

This section is written by hand from the results above, reading each program’s card (4e) with its Suzuki SNV counts (4c) and trait-profile similarity (4d). The calls are:

  • clear: the SNV counts favour the cluster (q ≤ 0.05) and the trait profile is closest to it or to a cluster it cannot be told apart from;
  • partial: only one of the two supports the cluster, or the program sits between two similar clusters;
  • none: no consistent match.

Three pairs of clusters have similar profiles over the traits GPMap has (4d): Beta cell +PI and −PI (cosine 0.92), Metabolic syndrome and Lipodystrophy (0.81), and Body fat and Obesity (0.73). A program is not expected to separate the members of a pair, so a call can name both.

The program numbers and statistics below come from one render. The next chunk checks each call against the current results and prints a warning if a program has changed, so the text cannot silently go stale.

Hand-written match of each high (green) or medium (orange) program to Suzuki’s clusters
program suzuki_cluster call reading
1 Obesity clear Largest program. Most of its matched SNVs are Obesity (SEC16B, TFAP2B, GNPDA2, BDNF, FTO) and its profile is closest to Obesity. Its most specific traits (education, intelligence, apolipoprotein B) are not Suzuki traits.
11 Beta cell +PI / Beta cell -PI clear The only beta-cell program. HbA1c is its most specific glycaemic trait, it carries CDC123/CAMK1D, CDKN2A/B and KCNJ11/ABCC8, and its SNVs lean to Beta cell -PI while its profile is closest to Beta cell +PI. The two clusters are not separable here, as expected.
49 Obesity clear A compact BMI core: BMI, body size at age 10 and impedance. Most of its SNPs are also in P1, including SEC16B, GNPDA2 and TFAP2B.
6 Lipodystrophy / Metabolic syndrome clear GRB14/COBLL1, INSR and ARL15; SHBG, heel bone density and lean mass. Lipodystrophy SNVs are the most over-represented and Metabolic syndrome SNVs the most numerous; the profile is closest to Lipodystrophy.
2 Lipodystrophy clear A lipid (VLDL, triglyceride) program at the insulin-resistance loci (INSR, GRB14/COBLL1, ANKRD55, CMIP). P33 and P36 sit inside it.
  ↳ 33 Lipodystrophy / Metabolic syndrome partial Sub-program of P2 with 4 SNPs: triglycerides and HDL. Too few SNPs for the SNV counts; the profile matches Lipodystrophy.
    ↳ 36 Lipodystrophy / Metabolic syndrome partial Sub-program of P33 with 3 SNPs. Too few SNPs for the SNV counts; the profile matches Lipodystrophy.
54 Lipodystrophy / Metabolic syndrome partial HDL and triglycerides with KLF14; the profile matches Lipodystrophy but its 6 SNPs show no cluster preference.
44 Obesity clear Obesity SNVs and an Obesity profile, with C-reactive protein as its most specific trait: an inflammation-flavoured obesity program.
40 none none Three SNPs in the MHC region with immune pathways; not a Suzuki-like program.
22 Obesity / Body fat partial CRP and limb fat percentage; the profile is closest to Obesity, but the SNV counts show no preference.
50 Beta cell +PI / Beta cell -PI partial MTNR1B, a fasting-glucose locus, with triglycerides and GGT. Its profile is closest to Beta cell +PI, but the SNV preference is not significant.
16 Obesity clear Obesity SNVs (SEC16B, TFAP2B, GNPDA2, PCSK1) and an Obesity profile; shares many SNPs with P1.
4 Obesity clear Second large Obesity program (education, sitting height, triglycerides); shares many SNPs with P1.
13 none none Mixed: alcohol intake, LDL and pulse pressure. The profile sits between Lipodystrophy and Metabolic syndrome, but the SNVs show no preference.
31 Lipodystrophy / Metabolic syndrome clear Blood pressure and impedance at GRB14/COBLL1, EBF1 and CYTL1; Lipodystrophy SNVs over-represented and a Lipodystrophy profile.
10 Metabolic syndrome / Lipodystrophy clear Red-cell traits and triglycerides at INSR, ABO and GRB14/COBLL1; Metabolic syndrome SNVs over-represented, Lipodystrophy profile.
26 none none Six SNPs, HDL and triglycerides; no SNV preference and no clear profile.
35 Metabolic syndrome / Lipodystrophy clear Platelet and red-cell traits with SHBG; Metabolic syndrome SNVs over-represented, Lipodystrophy profile.
24 Metabolic syndrome clear Lean mass and heel bone density; the strongest Metabolic syndrome SNV enrichment, and its profile is closest to Metabolic syndrome.
53 Lipodystrophy / Metabolic syndrome partial HDL cholesterol; a Lipodystrophy profile but no significant SNV preference.
17 Lipodystrophy / Metabolic syndrome partial Three SNPs, triglycerides; a Lipodystrophy profile, too few SNPs for the SNV counts.
45 none none Lung function and lean mass; no SNV preference, and the profile is only weakly Obesity-like.
47 Lipodystrophy / Metabolic syndrome clear IGF-1, AST and red-cell traits at PNPLA3 and INS/IGF2; Lipodystrophy SNVs over-represented, Metabolic syndrome profile.

Against the expectations.

  • Obesity is recovered clearly and repeatedly (P1, P49, P44, P16, P4). P1, P4 and P16 share many SNPs, and P49 is a BMI core that sits mostly inside P1.
  • Lipodystrophy and Metabolic syndrome are recovered together. Many programs sit at the insulin-resistance loci (GRB14/COBLL1, INSR, ANKRD55, CMIP, KLF14). The SNV counts pull some towards Lipodystrophy (P2, P6, P31, P47) and others towards Metabolic syndrome (P10, P24, P35). The trait profiles cannot separate the two, because Suzuki’s own profiles are close over these traits.
  • Beta cell: one joint program (P11), as expected. It carries markers of both beta-cell clusters, and neither the SNVs nor the profile split them.
  • Body fat merges into Obesity, as expected. No program prefers Body fat SNVs; they are spread over the Obesity programs.
  • Residual glycaemic, the largest cluster, has no program of its own. Its SNVs are spread across programs (4c), which fits its role as a catch-all.
  • Liver/lipid metabolism is not recovered, as expected with 3 signals.
  • Tissues give little support to the expectations. Only four high or medium programs have a loading-based tissue hit (4e). P35 (Metabolic syndrome / Lipodystrophy) is enriched in liver, P22 and P17 in plasma, and P26 (no match) in kidney cortex and brain amygdala. No Lipodystrophy-like program is enriched in adipose, and no Obesity program in brain.

Part 5: Candidate trait pairs for a multi-trait analysis

This part is documentation only; nothing here is run. Each pair runs the upload against one partner trait in the multi-trait investigation. The Suzuki clusters predict which shared programs the pair should show and in which direction:

  • concordant: the T2D risk allele raises the partner trait;
  • antagonistic: the T2D risk allele lowers it.
Partner trait GPMap id N Coloc groups Clusters it should separate Expected pattern
Body mass index 1992 532,396 992 Obesity vs beta-cell Obesity programs shared and concordant; Beta cell ±PI programs T2D-specific
Triglyceride levels 1631 437,532 587 Lipodystrophy, Metabolic syndrome, Liver/lipid Lipodystrophy and Metabolic syndrome concordant; TM6SF2-type liver loci antagonistic
HDL cholesterol levels 1630 400,754 735 Lipodystrophy, Obesity, Metabolic syndrome Antagonistic sharing (T2D risk lowers HDL)
Waist-to-hip ratio adjusted for BMI 1653 458,349 478 Lipodystrophy vs Obesity Lipodystrophy concordant, with BMI removed
Waist-hip ratio 1994 502,773 550 Lipodystrophy, Obesity, Metabolic syndrome Concordant for all three
Haemoglobin A1c levels 1640 437,749 838 Beta-cell, Residual glycaemic Glycaemic clusters shared; obesity/lipid clusters weaker
Fasting glucose 913 200,622 95 Beta-cell, Residual glycaemic As HbA1c, but sparse in GPMap
Body fat percentage 2581 401,772 671 Body fat, Obesity vs Lipodystrophy Body fat and Obesity concordant; Lipodystrophy antagonistic
Alanine aminotransferase / GGT 1642 / 1634 ≈437,700 449 / 702 Liver/lipid, Metabolic syndrome Liver-fat loci concordant
Coronary artery disease 2475 352,063 64 Obesity vs Beta cell +PI Obesity concordant; Beta cell +PI antagonistic (Suzuki’s polygenic-score result)
Type 2 diabetes (GPMap native) 114 655,666 178 none Replication pair: programs should correspond one to one

Caveat: sample overlap. UK Biobank, and for several traits FinnGen and the Million Veteran Program, contribute to both the T2DGGI EUR meta-analysis and most partner GWAS. Correlated sampling error then inflates apparent sharing between the two traits. Sharing that is weak or confined to a single locus should be read with this in mind.

Untested. The multi-trait vignette has not yet been run with an upload GUID as one of its traits. A first run would look like this:

  ),
  output_file = "investigation-multitrait-programs-t2dggi-bmi.html"
